questions.stem:
Two tunnels are planned to be dug through Sydney’s Blue Mountains to improve traffic infrastructure.

Digging at one end of the tunnel is to begin at the point \((-9,\ 15,\ 7)\) at Blackheath and continue in the direction \(7\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}\). The digging at the other end of the tunnel will start at the coordinate \((33,\ 5,\ -1)\) near Springwood and continue in the direction \(-14\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{k}\). Both sections are to be straight lines.

The coordinates are measured relative to a fixed origin \(O\), where one unit is 500 metres.

parts.stem: Show that the two sections of the tunnel will eventually meet at a point near Wentworth Falls and find the coordinates of this point.
parts.hint: Equate the components of the two vector equations; solve j and k first, then check i.

steps.explain: Write a vector equation for each section.
If they meet, all three components are equal for some \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\).
Solve the two simple equations first.
Check the \(\mathbf{i}\) equation with these values. It is satisfied, so the lines really do meet.
Substitute \(\lambda=2\) to get the meeting point.

parts.stem: Show that the points \(L(-5,6,-5)\), \(M(7,-2,-1)\) and \(N(10,-4,0)\) are collinear.
parts.hint: Show LM is a multiple of MN.

steps.explain: Find \(\overrightarrow{LM}\).
Find \(\overrightarrow{MN}\).
Compare.
The vectors are parallel and share the point \(M\), so \(L\), \(M\), \(N\) lie on one line.

parts.answer: \(\overrightarrow{LM}=12\mathbf{i}-8\mathbf{j}+4\mathbf{k}=4(3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})\), \(\overrightarrow{MN}=3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\). So LM = 4MN: parallel with common point M, hence collinear.

keyPoints.note: Parallel vectors with a common point are on one line.

parts.stem: Hence find the ratio in which \(M\) divides \(LN\).
parts.hint: Use LM = 4MN.

steps.explain: From (i), \(\overrightarrow{LM}=4\overrightarrow{MN}\): \(LM\) is 4 times as long as \(MN\), in the same direction.
So \(M\) divides \(LN\) internally in the ratio \(4:1\).

keyPoints.note: The ratio is LM : MN.

parts.answer: First component: −3 + 2λ = 7 ⇒ λ = 5. Then y = 5 − 5 = 0 ✓, z = −1 + 15 = 14 ✓. So (7, 0, 14) is on the line.

questions.stem: The equations of two lines are; \(\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -3\\ 1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 4\\ 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\ 6\\ -2\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}4\\ -11\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\)

parts.stem: Explain why these lines are not parallel.
parts.hint: Parallel ⇔ direction vectors are scalar multiples.

steps.explain: Lines are parallel exactly when their direction vectors are multiples of each other.
If \((4,-11,3)=k(1,4,1)\) then \(k=4\) from the first component, but \(4\times4=16\neq-11\). No such \(k\).
So the lines are not parallel. (Different position vectors or lengths don't decide it; a non-zero dot product only shows they aren't perpendicular.)

options: Their direction vectors have different lengths.
The dot product of the direction vectors is not zero.
The direction vectors \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 4\\ 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\ -11\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\) are not scalar multiples of each other.

keyPoints.note: Check whether (4, −11, 3) is a multiple of (1, 4, 1).

parts.stem: Determine whether these lines are skew or whether they intersect.
parts.hint: Solve two component equations for λ and μ, then test the third.

steps.explain: Equate the components.

Only one intersection ⇒ this quadratic in λ has one (repeated) root, so λ = −B/(2A) = \(-\frac{2\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c})}{2|\mathbf{b}|^2}=\frac{\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})}{|\mathbf{b}|^2}\).

The point of contact (which is also the radius vector, since the centre is \(O\)):
Dot with the tangent's direction \(\mathbf{m}\), using \(\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{m}=1\).

parts.answer: For a tangent Δ = 0, i.e. \(a^2=\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{b}-(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{m})^2\); the quadratic becomes \((\lambda+\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{m})^2=0\), so λ = −b·m. The contact point is \(\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{b}-(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{m})\mathbf{m}\). Then \(\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{b}-(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{m})(\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{m})=0\). So the radius p is perpendicular to the tangent direction m.

questions.stem:
Three different particles move in the \(xy\)-plane according to trajectories defined parametrically by:
\(\mathbf{R}_1(t)=\cos(t)\mathbf{i}+\sin(t)\mathbf{j}\)
\(\mathbf{R}_2(t)=\cos(2t)\mathbf{i}+\sin(2t)\mathbf{j}\)
\(\mathbf{R}_3(t)=\sin(t)\mathbf{i}+\cos(t)\mathbf{j}\)

For each particle, describe:
1. the shape of the path
2. the period of the motion
3. the direction of the motion
questions.hint: Check x² + y², the time to repeat, and where each particle goes from t = 0.

steps.explain: Shape: each has \(x^2+y^2=1\) (e.g. \(\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1\)), so all three paths are the unit circle.
Period: \(\mathbf R_1\) and \(\mathbf R_3\) repeat when \(t\) increases by \(2\pi\); \(\mathbf R_2\) uses \(2t\), so it repeats twice as fast.

Direction: track the start and a quarter-period later. \(\mathbf R_1\): \((1,0)\to(0,1)\) — anticlockwise. \(\mathbf R_2\): \((1,0)\to(0,1)\) at \(t=\frac\pi4\) — anticlockwise. \(\mathbf R_3\): \((0,1)\to(1,0)\) — clockwise.

questions.stem: Let \(\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\ -2\\ 6\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix}-2m\\ 2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}\), where \(m\) is a real constant. For what value of \(m\) will the vector \(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}\) be perpendicular to the vector \(\mathbf{b}\)?

Perpendicular means the dot product is zero.

questions.answer: Since the angle between \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) is \(90^\circ\), \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\). questions.answer: Let \(\overrightarrow{AM}=\mathbf{p}\) and \(\overrightarrow{MB}=\mathbf{q}\).
